paras: The attempted lynching of Robert Bishop occurred on the night of September 11, 1903, at a railroad graders' camp at Oakville, St. Louis County, Missouri, when fellow graders tried to hang Bishop, a Black worker accused of shooting two people. Bishop escaped, and a Ste. Genevieve County posse later shot a Black man taken for him who, the local paper said, proved to be the wrong man.
Charles A. Waddell, foreman of the construction crew, told St. Louis police that Bishop had shot Sam Ellis and a woman known as "Black Ida" at the camp, and blamed jealousy.

According to the St. Louis Republic, the other graders tried to hang Bishop and chased him for a mile. Frightened by the threats, he ran to St. Louis with Waddell following, then escaped south through the forests along the Mississippi.

Acting on a description circulated by Constable John Schaper of Carondelet Township, the Ste. Genevieve County sheriff organized a posse. The Republic, citing the sheriff's office at Clayton, said Bishop fired a revolver at the posse and was shot four times. Fair Play of Ste. Genevieve instead said Sheriff Berry's posse shot a Black man who ran from Burke's camp near Little Rock landing, and captured him the next day at St. Mary's.

When Schaper came to identify the prisoner, Fair Play reported, "he proved to be the wrong man," though he was held on a concealed-weapons charge. No report was found of any action against the graders or of Bishop's arrest.

The Republic treated the case as a police story under the headlines "TRAILS NEGRO TO ST. LOUIS" and "NEGRO WOUNDED BY POSSE," mentioning the attempted hanging only as the reason Bishop fled. Fair Play ran the posse's "desperate battle with a negro" among its local briefs. No Black-press coverage was found.

The Republic said three bullets struck Black Ida, while Fair Play said Bishop had "shot and killed" her. On whom the posse shot, Fair Play's later, local report of Schaper's identification is the better evidence.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Bishop
bases: Graders at the Oakville camp tried to hang Robert Bishop, a Black man accused of a shooting, and chased him a mile with that purpose; he escaped, so the lynching was attempted, not completed (A1, A2).

The 'other graders' acted without legal authority to punish Bishop for the shooting he was accused of, but he escaped and no one was killed by them (A1, A2); their number is not given. The man later wounded by the Ste. Genevieve posse survived (A2, A3).

Only the St. Louis Republic reports the lynching threat and the attempted hanging (A1, A2); the Ste. Genevieve Fair Play independently reports the shooting at Oakville and the manhunt but not the lynching attempt, and it says the man captured was not Bishop (A3).

accounts.label: Foreman's report to police
accounts.gist: Waddell told the police Bishop shot Ellis and Black Ida out of jealousy and that lynching threats frightened him into running to the city.

accounts.label: Clayton sheriff's office information
accounts.gist: The graders tried to hang Bishop; he was later found in bushes near Ste. Genevieve, fired a revolver at the posse, and was shot four times and hospitalized.

accounts.label: Ste. Genevieve local report
accounts.gist: A Black man seen at Burke's camp ran when told to surrender, was shot, escaped, was captured next day at St. Mary's, and proved not to be Bishop.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Republic told the story as a police matter ('TRAILS NEGRO TO ST. LOUIS', 'Sheriff Captures Robert Bishop After Desperate Fight'), mentioning the attempted hanging only as the reason he fled.
Fair Play ran the posse's 'desperate battle with a negro' among local briefs and reported plainly that the wounded man was the wrong man.

versions.value: Wounded: three bullets penetrated her body (no death stated)

conflicts.note: The Republic's account comes from the foreman the next day; Fair Play's comes from the alert sent from Oakville to Ste. Genevieve. Neither reports an inquest.

conflicts.field: identity of the man shot by the posse

versions.value: Not Bishop: 'the wrong man', identified by Constable Schaper

conflicts.note: Fair Play is the later, local report and describes the identification the Republic said was about to take place, so it is the better evidence on this point.

versions.value: Found in bushes on the outskirts of Ste. Genevieve, drew a .41-caliber revolver, shot four times, taken to a hospital; captured 'yesterday' (September 16)
Found at Burke's camp near Little Rock landing on Sunday morning, ran and was shot, escaped, captured next day at St. Mary's and jailed

conflicts.note: The two accounts probably describe the same posse encounter; the Republic's came secondhand through the sheriff's office at Clayton.

in pursuit: chased a mile immediately after the shooting
0 in the lynching attempt; Fair Play says Black Ida was killed in the shooting Bishop was accused of, the Republic says only that she was shot
Should add that a Ste. Genevieve posse shot a Black man taken for Bishop, whom the local paper says proved to be the wrong man

info: Shooting and attempted lynching on Friday night, September 11, 1903
Robert Bishop, described as 'a negro', target of the attempted hanging
Accused of shooting Sam Ellis (in the shoulder and hip) and a woman known as 'Black Ida' (three bullets); the foreman attributed it to jealousy
'The other graders' at the camp; their race is not stated
No report of any action against the graders, or of the arrest of the real Bishop, was found

sources.note: First report, from foreman Charles A. Waddell to First District police: Bishop shot Sam Ellis and 'Black Ida' at the Oakville camp Friday night; lynching threats drove him to the city; not yet arrested.
quotes: Threats of lynching the negro. Bishop, frightened him, and he ran all the way to the city, with Waddell close behind, watching him.
